items.title: Unitary conjugation, generator transport and strong commutation of self-adjoint observables
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of
Dependent Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral and
Bochner suppliers. Fix $\hbar>0$, let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space
([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $K$ and $A$ be self-adjoint operators on $H$ with
spectral projection-valued measures $E_K$ and $E_A$
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]), let $W\in\mathcal B(H)$ be unitary
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), and put
$$U_K(t):=e^{-itK/\hbar},\qquad U_A(s):=e^{-isA/\hbar}\qquad(s,t\in\mathbb R)$$
in the spectral calculus of [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]], which are
strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups
([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]],
[[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). Write
$\Phi_K(g)=\int g\,dE_K$ for bounded Borel $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$
([[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]), and let
$K_W:=WKW^{*}$ with $D(K_W):=WD(K)$. Then:

(a) $K_W$ is self-adjoint with spectral projection-valued measure
$$E_{K_W}(B)=WE_K(B)W^{*}\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
its flow satisfies $e^{-itK_W/\hbar}=WU_K(t)W^{*}$ for every $t$, and the
conjugated family $s\mapsto WU_A(s)W^{*}$ is a strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group whose infinitesimal generator is
$-\frac{i}{\hbar}WAW^{*}$ with domain $WD(A)$
([[def-infinitesimal-generator-of-a-unitary-group]]);

(b) the following are equivalent:

  (i) $U_A(s)U_K(t)=U_K(t)U_A(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$;

  (ii) $E_A(B)E_K(C)=E_K(C)E_A(B)$ for all Borel sets $B,C\subseteq\mathbb R$;

  (iii) $U_K(t)D(A)=D(A)$ and $U_K(t)AU_K(t)^{*}=A$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$;

(c) if a bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ satisfies $BU_K(t)=U_K(t)B$ for every
$t\in\mathbb R$, then $B\Phi_K(g)=\Phi_K(g)B$ for every bounded Borel
$g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$; in particular $BE_K(C)=E_K(C)B$ for every Borel
$C\subseteq\mathbb R$;

(d) if (i)-(iii) of (b) hold, then $E_A(B)U_K(t)=U_K(t)E_A(B)$ for every Borel
$B\subseteq\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of
Dependent Choice; $\hbar>0$; a nonzero complex Hilbert space $H$; self-adjoint
$K,A$ with spectral PVMs $E_K,E_A$; a unitary $W$; the flows $U_K,U_A$;
bounded Borel functions $g,h$; vectors $x,y\in H$; real $s,t$; Borel sets
$B,C\subseteq\mathbb R$.

[F1] **Flow calculus.** For a self-adjoint operator $L$ with spectral PVM $E_L$
and flow $U_L(\tau)=e^{-i\tau L/\hbar}$: $U_L$ is a strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group with $U_L(\tau)^{*}=U_L(-\tau)$, $U_L(\tau)D(L)=D(L)$
and $LU_L(\tau)=U_L(\tau)L$ on $D(L)$; the difference quotient
$\frac1\tau\bigl(U_L(\tau)x-x\bigr)$ converges as $\tau\to0$ exactly for
$x\in D(L)$, with limit $-\frac{i}{\hbar}Lx$; and for bounded Borel $f$ one has
$f(L)U_L(\tau)=U_L(\tau)f(L)$ with $f(L)=\Phi_{E_L}(f)$
([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]],
[[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]],
[[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]).

[F2] **Spectral calculus.** $\Phi_{E_L}$ is a unital $\ast$-homomorphism from
the bounded Borel functions to $\mathcal B(H)$, $\|\Phi_{E_L}(f)\|\le\sup|f|$,
$E_L(B)=\Phi_{E_L}(\mathbf 1_B)$, and the map $B\mapsto E_L(B)$ is a regular
projection-valued measure whose scalar measures $\langle E_L(\cdot)x,x\rangle$
are finite regular Borel measures
([[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]],
[[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]],
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]],
[[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]).

[F3] **Uniqueness of the spectral measure.** If a regular projection-valued
measure $F$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$ satisfies $\int\lambda\,dF(\lambda)x=Lx$
for all $x\in D(L)$ and $D(L)=\{x:\int\lambda^2\,dF_x(\lambda)<\infty\}$, then
$F=E_L$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]).

[F4] **Stone's theorem.** $T\mapsto e^{itT}$ is a bijection from the self-adjoint
operators onto the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups; two such
groups that agree at every real time have the same values, hence the same
generator, and a group is determined by its generator
([[thm-stone-one-parameter-unitary-groups]],
[[def-infinitesimal-generator-of-a-unitary-group]]).

[F5] **Laplace resolvents.** For a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary
group $U$ with infinitesimal generator $G$ and $\lambda>0$, the Bochner integral
$Q_\pm(\lambda)=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}U(\pm t)\,dt$ is a bounded operator
with $\|Q_\pm(\lambda)\|\le1/\lambda$ and
$(\lambda\mp G)Q_\pm(\lambda)=I$, $Q_\pm(\lambda)(\lambda\mp G)=I$ on $D(G)$;
bounded linear maps commute with Bochner integrals
([[lem-laplace-resolvents-of-a-unitary-group]],
[[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]).

[F6] **Density of the resolvent algebra.** For a closed nonempty $K\subseteq\mathbb R$
the $\ast$-subalgebra generated by the single function $\lambda\mapsto(\lambda-z)^{-1}$,
$z\in\mathbb C\setminus K$, is dense in the algebra $C_\infty(K)$ of continuous
functions vanishing at infinity; and for a finite Radon measure $\mu$ on
$\mathbb R$ the space $C_c(\mathbb R)\subseteq C_\infty(\mathbb R)$ is dense in
$L^p(\mu)$ for $1\le p<\infty$
([[thm-complex-stone-weierstrass-self-adjoint]],
[[thm-c-c-is-dense-in-l-p-for-radon-measures]]).


## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; transport the spectral data through the unitary
conjugation, prove the equivalence (i) - (iii) by comparing generators of
conjugated groups, and obtain the commutation with spectral projections through
the Laplace resolvent and the density of the resolvent algebra.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F6].

1.1 [Well-definedness, density and symmetry of $K_W$] The domain $D(K_W)=WD(K)$ is a linear subspace, dense in $H$ because $D(K)$ is dense and $W$ is surjective, and $K_Wx=WKW^{*}x$ is defined and linear on it. For $x=Wu$, $y=Wv$ with $u,v\in D(K)$ one has $\langle K_Wx,y\rangle=\langle KWu,Wv\rangle=\langle Ku,v\rangle=\langle u,Kv\rangle=\langle x,K_Wy\rangle$ because $W$ is unitary and $K$ is symmetric; hence $K_W$ is symmetric. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 [(ii) implies (i)] Assume (ii). For simple Borel functions $g=\sum_ic_i\mathbf 1_{B_i}$ and $h=\sum_jd_j\mathbf 1_{C_j}$ the identities $E_A(B_i)E_K(C_j)=E_K(C_j)E_A(B_i)$ give $\Phi_A(g)\Phi_K(h)=\sum_{i,j}c_id_jE_A(B_i)E_K(C_j)=\sum_{i,j}c_id_jE_K(C_j)E_A(B_i)=\Phi_K(h)\Phi_A(g)$. Given bounded Borel $g,h$, choose simple $g_n\to g$, $h_n\to h$ uniformly; then $\Phi_A(g_n)\to\Phi_A(g)$ and $\Phi_K(h_n)\to\Phi_K(h)$ in operator norm by [F2], so the identities pass to the limits, giving $\Phi_A(g)\Phi_K(h)=\Phi_K(h)\Phi_A(g)$. Taking $g(\lambda)=e^{-is\lambda/\hbar}$ and $h(\mu)=e^{-it\mu/\hbar}$ and applying [F2] gives $U_A(s)U_K(t)=U_K(t)U_A(s)$ for all $s,t$, which is (i). [F2, given, algebra]

1.3 [Commutation with the flow implies commutation with the calculus] Let $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ satisfy $BU_K(t)=U_K(t)B$ for all $t$. Apply [F5] to the group $U_K$ and its generator $G_K=-\frac{i}{\hbar}K$ with $D(G_K)=D(K)$: for each $\lambda>0$ the Bochner integral $Q_+(\lambda)=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}U_K(t)\,dt$ equals $(\lambda-G_K)^{-1}$, and since the bounded linear maps $S\mapsto BS$ and $S\mapsto SB$ on $\mathcal B(H)$ commute with Bochner integration, $BQ_+(\lambda)=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}BU_K(t)\,dt=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}U_K(t)B\,dt=Q_+(\lambda)B$. The same argument with $U_K(-t)=U_K(t)^{*}$ gives $BQ_-(\lambda)=Q_-(\lambda)B$ for $Q_-(\lambda)=(\lambda+G_K)^{-1}=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}U_K(-t)\,dt$. Now $Q_+(\lambda)=(\lambda+\frac{i}{\hbar}K)^{-1}=\frac{\hbar}{i}(K-i\hbar\lambda)^{-1}$ and $Q_-(\lambda)=(\lambda-\frac{i}{\hbar}K)^{-1}=i\hbar(K+i\hbar\lambda)^{-1}$ are nonzero scalar multiples of the resolvents of $K$ at $i\hbar\lambda$ and $-i\hbar\lambda$; choosing $\lambda=1$ shows that $B$ commutes with the functions $g_\pm(\mu)=(\mu\pm i\hbar)^{-1}$ and hence with every polynomial in $g_+,g_-$ and their conjugates, that is with every element of the $\ast$-subalgebra generated by $g_+$. [F5, given, algebra]

2.1 [Adjoint and self-adjointness] Let $y\in D(K_W^{*})$ and put $z=K_W^{*}y$. For every $u\in D(K)$ the vector $Wu$ lies in $D(K_W)$ with $K_W(Wu)=WKu$, so $\langle Ku,W^{*}y\rangle=\langle WKu,y\rangle=\langle K_W(Wu),y\rangle=\langle Wu,z\rangle=\langle u,W^{*}z\rangle$; the functional $u\mapsto\langle Ku,W^{*}y\rangle$ is therefore bounded on $D(K)$, whence $W^{*}y\in D(K^{*})=D(K)$ and $K^{*}W^{*}y=KW^{*}y=W^{*}z$. Applying the unitary $W$ gives $y\in WD(K)=D(K_W)$ and $K_Wy=z$. Hence $D(K_W^{*})\subseteq D(K_W)$ with agreement there, and with step 1.1 the operator $K_W$ is self-adjoint. [step 1.1, F1, given, algebra]

2.2 [Continuous vanishing functions] Let $f\in C_\infty(\sigma(K))$, a closed subset of $\mathbb R$. By [F6] there are elements $p_n$ of the $\ast$-subalgebra generated by $\mu\mapsto(\mu-i\hbar)^{-1}$ with $\sup_{\sigma(K)}|p_n-f|\to0$. Each $p_n(K)=\Phi_K(p_n)$ commutes with $B$ by step 1.3, and $\|\Phi_K(p_n)-\Phi_K(f)\|\le\sup_{\sigma(K)}|p_n-f|\to0$ by the norm bound of [F2], so $\Phi_K(f)$ commutes with $B$. [step 1.3, F2, F6, algebra]

3.1 [Spectral measure transport] Put $F(B):=WE_K(B)W^{*}$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R$. Each $F(B)$ is an orthogonal projection as the conjugate of one; $F(\varnothing)=0$ and $F(\mathbb R)=I$; finite additivity and strong countable additivity follow from those of $E_K$ and boundedness of $W$; and $F$ is regular because its scalar measure in $x$ is $\langle F(B)x,x\rangle=\langle E_K(B)W^{*}x,W^{*}x\rangle$, which is a finite regular Borel measure by [F2]. For $x=Wu$ with $u\in D(K)$ one has $\int\lambda\,dF_x(\lambda)=\langle\int\lambda\,dE_K(\lambda)W^{*}x,W^{*}x\rangle=\langle Ku,u\rangle=\langle WKu,Wu\rangle=\langle K_Wx,x\rangle$ by the calculus of [F2], and $\int\lambda^2\,dF_x(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $u\in D(K)$, that is exactly when $x\in D(K_W)$; hence $F$ represents $K_W$ and [F3] gives $F=E_{K_W}$. [step 2.1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

3.2 [Bounded Borel functions] Let $g$ be bounded Borel and fix $x\in H$. The scalar measure $\mu_x:=E_{K,x}$ is a finite regular Borel measure by [F2], so by [F6] there are $f_n\in C_c(\mathbb R)\subseteq C_\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\int|g-f_n|^2\,d\mu_x\to0$; then $\|(\Phi_K(g)-\Phi_K(f_n))x\|^2=\int|g-f_n|^2\,d\mu_x\to0$ by [F2]. Since $\Phi_K(f_n)$ commutes with $B$ by step 2.2, $$\|\,[B,\Phi_K(g)]x\,\|\le\|B\|\,\|(\Phi_K(g)-\Phi_K(f_n))x\|+\|(\Phi_K(g)-\Phi_K(f_n))Bx\|\longrightarrow0,$$ using boundedness of $B$; hence $B\Phi_K(g)=\Phi_K(g)B$. Taking $g=\mathbf 1_C$ and using $E_K(C)=\Phi_K(\mathbf 1_C)$ from [F2] gives $BE_K(C)=E_K(C)B$. This proves (c). [step 2.2, F2, F6, given, algebra]

4.1 [Flow and generator transport] By [F2] applied to the bounded Borel functions $f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}$, $e^{-itK_W/\hbar}=\Phi_{E_{K_W}}(f_t)=W\Phi_{E_K}(f_t)W^{*}=WU_K(t)W^{*}$, which is the displayed flow identity. For $x\in D(K_W)=WD(K)$, say $x=Wu$, the difference quotients of $s\mapsto WU_A(s)W^{*}$ at $0$ are $\frac1s\bigl(WU_A(s)u-u\bigr)=W\frac1s\bigl(U_A(s)u-u\bigr)$, which converge in $H$ because $W$ is an isometry; by [F1] they converge exactly when $u\in D(A)$, and then to $W\bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}Au\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}WAW^{*}x$. If $x\notin D(K_W)$, then $u=W^{*}x\notin D(A)$ and the quotients do not converge: otherwise applying the bounded operator $W^{*}$ would make the quotients of $U_A$ at $u$ converge. Hence the conjugated group has infinitesimal generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}WAW^{*}$ with domain $WD(A)$, and it is strongly continuous because $W$ is bounded and $U_A$ is. This proves (a). [step 3.1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

4.2 [(iii) implies (ii)] Assume (iii) and fix $t$. By (iii), $U_K(t)AU_K(t)^{*}=A$; by uniqueness of the spectral measure [F3] and step 3.1 applied with $W=U_K(t)$, $$E_A(B)=E_{U_K(t)AU_K(t)^{*}}(B)=U_K(t)E_A(B)U_K(t)^{*}$$ for every Borel $B$, so $E_A(B)$ commutes with $U_K(t)$ and with $U_K(t)^{*}=U_K(-t)$. Since $E_A(B)$ is bounded and commutes with the flow $U_K$, step (c) with $B:=E_A(B)$ gives $E_A(B)\Phi_K(g)=\Phi_K(g)E_A(B)$ for every bounded Borel $g$; taking $g=\mathbf 1_C$ gives $E_A(B)E_K(C)=E_K(C)E_A(B)$, which is (ii). [step 3.1, step 1.3, step 3.2, F2, F3, given, algebra]

5.1 [(i) implies (iii)] Assume (i), fix $t\in\mathbb R$, and put $V(s):=U_K(t)^{*}U_A(s)U_K(t)$; by (i) $V(s)=U_A(s)$ for every $s$. The family $V$ is a strongly continuous unitary group, and by step 4.1 with $W=U_K(t)^{*}$ its infinitesimal generator is $-\frac{i}{\hbar}U_K(t)^{*}AU_K(t)$ with domain $U_K(t)^{*}D(A)$; the right-hand side $U_A$ has generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}A$ with domain $D(A)$ by [F1]. Since the two groups coincide, their generators coincide by [F4], so $U_K(t)^{*}D(A)=D(A)$ and $U_K(t)^{*}AU_K(t)=A$. Applying the unitary $U_K(t)$ on both sides gives $U_K(t)D(A)=D(A)$ and $U_K(t)AU_K(t)^{*}=A$, which is (iii). [step 4.1, F1, F4, given, algebra]

5.2 [(iii) implies (i)] Assume (iii) and fix $t$. Put $V(s):=U_K(t)^{*}U_A(s)U_K(t)$. By step 4.1 with $W=U_K(t)^{*}$, the generator of $V$ is $-\frac{i}{\hbar}U_K(t)^{*}AU_K(t)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}A$ with domain $U_K(t)^{*}D(A)=D(A)$, which is the generator of $U_A$ by [F1]; hence $V=U_A$ by [F4] and $U_A(s)U_K(t)=U_K(t)U_A(s)$ for all $s$. [step 4.1, F1, F4, given, algebra]

6.1 [Assembly] Steps 1.2, 5.1, 5.2 and 4.2 give the implications (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii), so the three conditions are equivalent, which is (b). Under these conditions, step 4.2 in its first display already gives $E_A(B)U_K(t)=U_K(t)E_A(B)$ for all Borel $B$ and all $t$, which is (d): the displayed identity $E_A(B)=U_K(t)E_A(B)U_K(t)^{*}$ multiplied on the right by $U_K(t)$ yields $E_A(B)U_K(t)=U_K(t)E_A(B)$. [step 1.2, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 4.2, algebra] ∎




## Remarks

- **Why the hypotheses are formulated with groups.** The equivalence of (i),
  (ii) and (iii) is the precise sense in which "a self-adjoint quantity
  commutes with the energy" may be used: strong commutation of the spectral
  measures, commutation of the flows, and invariance of the domain of the
  quantity under the flow. A formal commutator identity on a small domain is
  not among the equivalent conditions and is not used.
- **Choice.** The Axiom of Choice is the hypothesis of the spectral theorem and
  of Stone's theorem; Countable and Dependent Choice are the hypotheses of the
  Bochner and density suppliers used in clause (c).

items.title: The spatial rotation action on the component-valued wave-function space
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of
the cited spectral suppliers. Fix an integer $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$, let
$H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ with inner product linear in the
first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-hilbert-space]]), let $Q_{j},P_{k}$ be the componentwise position and
momentum operators ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]
clause (a)), and let $\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$
and $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the componentwise Schwartz and
Sobolev classes ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]],
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Let $SO(3)$ be the special orthogonal
group with its Euclidean topology ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]],
[[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]) and for $R\in SO(3)$ define, componentwise,
$$\bigl(U(R)f\bigr)_{l}(x):=f_{l}(R^{-1}x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^{3},\ l=1,\dots,r).$$
Let $U^{(r)}$ be the unitary momentum representation of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] and $M_R$ the bounded operator
on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$ given by $(M_Rg)(p):=g(R^{-1}p)$. Then:

(a) $U(R)$ is a well-defined unitary operator for every $R$, with
$U(I)=\mathrm{id}$, $U(RS)=U(R)U(S)$ and $U(R)^{-1}=U(R^{-1})$ for all
$R,S\in SO(3)$; and for every $f\in H^{(r)}$ the orbit map
$R\mapsto U(R)f$ is continuous on $SO(3)$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]).
Moreover $U(R)\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and
$U(R)W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})=W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$
for $m=1,2$;

(b) $U^{(r)}U(R)U^{(r)-1}=M_R$, and consequently
$$U(R)D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j}),\qquad U(R)Q_{j}U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l=1}^{3}R_{lj}Q_{l},\qquad U(R)D(P_{k})=D(P_{k}),\qquad U(R)P_{k}U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l=1}^{3}R_{lk}P_{l}$$
as operator identities including domains;

(c) with the free operator $H_{0}:=\frac{1}{2m_{0}}\sum_{k=1}^{3}P_{k}^{2}$ for a
parameter $m_{0}>0$, whose domain is $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$,
one has $U(R)H_{0}U(R)^{-1}=H_{0}$; and for a real bounded measurable
$V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$ with multiplier $M_{V}$ (multiplication by $V$)
and $V_{R}(x):=V(R^{-1}x)$ one has $U(R)M_{V}U(R)^{-1}=M_{V_{R}}$, so that
$U(R)H_{V}U(R)^{-1}=H_{V_{R}}$ for the free-plus-$V$ operator $H_{V}$ with
domain $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice; $r\ge1$;
$\hbar>0$; the space $H^{(r)}$; the componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$;
$R,S\in SO(3)$; $f\in H^{(r)}$; $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$; the momentum
unitary $U^{(r)}$ and the multipliers $M_R$; a real bounded measurable $V$.

[F1] **Componentwise kinematics.** $Q_{j},P_{k}$ are self-adjoint with domains
$D(Q_{j})=\{f:x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \forall l\}$, $D(P_{k})=\{f:D_{k}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \forall l\}$,
and on $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ one has $Q_{j}f=x_{j}f$, $P_{k}f=-i\hbar D_{k}f$
componentwise; $\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq D(Q_{j})\cap D(P_{k})$ and both
operators map $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ into itself
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clauses (a),(c),
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F2] **Momentum representation.** $U^{(r)}$ is unitary and satisfies
$U^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(M_{p_{k}})$ and $U^{(r)}P_{k}=M_{p_{k}}U^{(r)}$; on Schwartz
classes it acts by the componentwise Fourier transform with normalization
$(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}$, and it maps $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ onto itself
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] clauses (a),(b),
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (b),
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F3] **Substitution and components.** For an orthogonal $R$ and $f\in L^{1}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ one has $\int f(R^{-1}x)\,dx=\int f(y)\,dy$, because the linear substitution scales Lebesgue measure by $|\det R|=1$ ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]],
[[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]). A class $f=(f_{l})$ of $H^{(r)}$ is
determined by its components, and componentwise operations preserve the
$L^{2}$ norm: $\|f\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|^{2}$
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a),
[[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]).

[F4] **Schwartz calculus.** $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ means each component
$\psi_{l}$ is smooth with $\sup_{x}|x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\psi_{l}(x)|<\infty$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; hence each component and each of its
derivatives is bounded, and $\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$
([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]],
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). For a linear substitution
$A$ with $|A x|\le\|A\|\,|x|$, the chain rule gives
$\partial^{\beta}(\psi_{l}\circ A)(x)=\sum_{|\gamma|=|\beta|}c_{\gamma}\,\partial^{\gamma}\psi_{l}(Ax)$
with constants depending only on $A,\beta$, so the seminorms of
$\psi_{l}\circ A$ are bounded by finitely many seminorms of $\psi_{l}$; in
particular $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ is invariant under composition with a linear map.

[F5] **Sobolev and Fourier characterization.** $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)=\{g\in L^{2}:p_{k}g\in L^{2}\ \forall k\}$
and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)=\{g\in L^{2}:|p|^{2}g\in L^{2}\}$ under the
momentum variable $p=2\pi\hbar\xi$ of the normalization of [F2], with
$\|g\|_{W^{2,2}}$ equivalent to $\|(1+|p|^{2})g\|_{2}$
([[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]],
[[thm-plancherel]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F6] **Density and extension.** $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ is dense in $H^{(r)}$
([[lem-schwartz-space-is-dense-in-l-two]]); a bounded linear operator on a dense
subspace extends uniquely to the whole space with the same norm
([[thm-extension-of-a-bounded-map-from-a-dense-subspace]]); if a sequence
$g_n\to g$ pointwise and $|g_n|\le h$ with $h$ integrable, then
$\int g_n\to\int g$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]); and for
$u,v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ one has $|u\cdot v|\le|u|\,|v|$
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; define the rotation action componentwise, prove
unitarity and the representation property by orthogonal substitution, transport
the action to the momentum representation for the operator conjugations, and
obtain strong continuity from dominated convergence and density.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F6].

1.1 [Well-definedness and unitarity] Let $R\in SO(3)$. For a representative $f$ of a class in $H^{(r)}$ the function $x\mapsto f(R^{-1}x)$ is measurable and its components satisfy $\int|f_{l}(R^{-1}x)|^{2}dx=\int|f_{l}(y)|^{2}dy$ by [F3], so the assignment is well defined on classes, linear, and isometric; it is surjective with inverse given by $R^{-1}$ because composition with $R^{-1}$ undoes it on representatives, so $U(R)$ is a unitary operator and $U(R)^{-1}=U(R^{-1})$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 [Representation and Schwartz invariance] For $R,S\in SO(3)$ and $f$ one has $(U(R)U(S)f)_{l}(x)=(U(S)f)_{l}(R^{-1}x)=f_{l}(S^{-1}R^{-1}x)=f_{l}((RS)^{-1}x)=(U(RS)f)_{l}(x)$, since $(RS)^{-1}=S^{-1}R^{-1}$ by [F3]; and $U(I)=\mathrm{id}$. For $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ each component $\psi_{l}\circ R^{-1}$ is smooth with all seminorms finite by [F4] applied to $A=R^{-1}$, and the same argument with $R$ in place of $R^{-1}$ gives $U(R)\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$. [step 1.1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.2 [Conjugation of position] Let $f\in H^{(r)}$ and compute with the definition of step 1.1: $(U(R)Q_{j}U(R)^{-1}f)_{l}(x)=\bigl(Q_{j}U(R)^{-1}f\bigr)_{l}(R^{-1}x)=(R^{-1}x)_{j}(U(R)^{-1}f)_{l}(R^{-1}x)=\bigl(\sum_{l'}R_{l'j}x_{l'}\bigr)f_{l}(x)$, using $(R^{-1}x)_{j}=\sum_{l'}R_{l'j}x_{l'}$; this also shows that $x_{j}\bigl(U(R)^{-1}f\bigr)_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l$ exactly when $x_{l'}(U(R)f)_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l'$, because the two $3$-tuples of coordinate functions are related by the invertible matrix $R$. Hence $U(R)D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j})$ and $U(R)Q_{j}U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l'}R_{l'j}Q_{l'}$. [step 1.1, F1, given, algebra]

3.1 [Strong continuity] Let $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and $R_{0}\in SO(3)$. For $R$ in a bounded neighbourhood of $R_{0}$ one has $|R^{-1}x|\ge\tfrac12|x|$ and $|R_{0}^{-1}x|\ge\tfrac12|x|$, so with the radial majorant $h(x):=\sup_{|y|\ge|x|/2}\max_{l}|\psi_{l}(y)|$ one has $|(U(R)\psi-U(R_{0})\psi)_{l}(x)|^{2}\le 4h(x)^{2}$ for every $x$, where $h\in L^{2}$ because $\psi$ is Schwartz; moreover $(U(R)\psi)_{l}(x)\to(U(R_{0})\psi)_{l}(x)$ for every $x$ as $R\to R_{0}$, by continuity of $\psi_{l}$ and of $R\mapsto R^{-1}x$. Dominated convergence gives $\|U(R)\psi-U(R_{0})\psi\|\to0$, and for $\varepsilon/3$-close $\psi$ to $f$ in the sense of [F6] the triangle inequality and unitarity of step 1.1 give $\|U(R)f-U(R_{0})f\|\le2\|f-\psi\|+\|U(R)\psi-U(R_{0})\psi\|<\varepsilon$ for $R$ close to $R_{0}$; hence the orbit map is continuous. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, F6, given, algebra]

3.2 [Momentum-space form of the action] Let $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and compute componentwise for $p\in\mathbb R^{3}$, using the substitution $y=R^{-1}x$, $x=Ry$ of [F3] and $R^{\mathsf T}=R^{-1}$: $(U^{(r)}U(R)\psi)_{l}(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi_{l}(R^{-1}x)\,dx=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot Ry/\hbar}\psi_{l}(y)\,dy=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int e^{-iR^{\mathsf T}p\cdot y/\hbar}\psi_{l}(y)\,dy=(U^{(r)}\psi)_{l}(R^{-1}p)=(M_RU^{(r)}\psi)_{l}(p)$. Both $U^{(r)}U(R)U^{(r)-1}$ and $M_R$ are bounded operators (products of unitaries), and they agree on the dense subspace $U^{(r)}\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$ of [F2]; [F6] extends the identity to all of $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F6, given, algebra]

4.1 [Sobolev invariance] By [F2] and [F5], $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ are the sets of classes $f$ with $p_{k}U^{(r)}f\in L^{2}$ for every $k$, respectively with $|p|^{2}U^{(r)}f\in L^{2}$; by step 3.2, $U^{(r)}U(R)f=(M_RU^{(r)}f)(p)=U^{(r)}f(R^{-1}p)$, and substitution of $R^{-1}p$ leaves the conditions $p_{k}g\in L^{2}$ and $|p|^{2}g\in L^{2}$ unchanged because $|R^{-1}p|=|p|$ and the coordinate functions are permuted by the orthogonal matrix; hence $U(R)W^{m,2}=W^{m,2}$ for $m=1,2$. [step 3.2, F2, F5, given, algebra]

4.2 [Conjugation of momentum] By [F2] and step 3.2, the conjugate of $P_{k}$ corresponds to $M_RM_{p_{k}}M_R^{-1}$, and for $g\in L^{2}$ with $p_{k}g\in L^{2}$ one has $(M_RM_{p_{k}}M_R^{-1}g)(p)=p_{k}(M_R^{-1}g)(Rp)$ with $(M_R^{-1}g)(Rp)=g(p)$, so $M_RM_{p_{k}}M_R^{-1}=M_{p_{k}\circ R^{-1}}=M_{\sum_{l}R_{lk}p_{l}}$: indeed $p_{k}(R^{-1}p)=\sum_{l}R_{lk}p_{l}$ because $(R^{-1})_{kl}=R_{lk}$. Hence $U(R)P_{k}U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l}R_{lk}P_{l}$ as self-adjoint operators including domains, the conjugates of $P_{k}$ under the unitaries $U^{(r)}$ and $U(R)$ being computed by the identities of [F2] and step 3.2. [step 3.2, F2, given, algebra]

5.1 [Free operator and multipliers] Since $U(R)P_{k}U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l}R_{lk}P_{l}$ with domain preservation by step 4.2 and $U(R)W^{2,2}=W^{2,2}$ by step 4.1, also $U(R)P_{k}^{2}U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l,l'}R_{lk}R_{l'k}P_{l}P_{l'}$ on $W^{2,2}$; summing over $k$ and using $\sum_{k}R_{lk}R_{l'k}=\delta_{ll'}$ for orthogonal $R$ gives $U(R)\bigl(\sum_{k}P_{k}^{2}\bigr)U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l}P_{l}^{2}$, so $U(R)H_{0}U(R)^{-1}=H_{0}$. For $f\in H^{(r)}$ one has $(U(R)M_{V}U(R)^{-1}f)_{l}(x)=V(R^{-1}x)f_{l}(x)$ by step 1.1, so $U(R)M_{V}U(R)^{-1}=M_{V_{R}}$ on all of $H^{(r)}$; adding the two identities on the common domain $W^{2,2}$ gives $U(R)H_{V}U(R)^{-1}=H_{V_{R}}$, which is (c). [step 4.1, step 4.2, F1, given, algebra]

6.1 [Assembly] Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 prove unitarity, the representation property, the Schwartz invariance, strong continuity and, with step 4.1, the Sobolev invariance of (a); steps 3.2, 4.2, 2.2 prove (b); step 5.1 proves (c). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 2.2, step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Convention.** With $U(R)f=f\circ R^{-1}$ the position operator transforms with the inverse matrix, $U(R)Q_{j}U(R)^{-1}=\sum_{l}R_{lj}Q_{l}$; this is exactly the conjugation identity computed in Binney's (4.26) with $U^{\dagger}(\alpha)xU(\alpha)=R(\alpha)x$. The invariant statement used by the physics items is the multiplier identity $U(R)M_{V}U(R)^{-1}=M_{V\circ R^{-1}}$ and the criterion $V\circ R^{-1}=V$.
- **Scope.** The lemma concerns the spatial factor only. No rotation action on the internal factor $\mathbb C^{r}$ and no SU(2) lift are introduced; those belong to the orbital-and-spin development.

B. Zwiebach, MIT 8.05 Quantum Physics II (Fall 2013), Chapter 9 'Angular Momentum', Section 1.2, printed pages 6-9 (PDF pages 6-9): the angular momentum operators, their commutation relations with position and momentum, and operators that are vectors under rotations

G. Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 1st edition 2009, Section 8.2, printed pages 175-177 (PDF pages 187-189): the one-parameter unitary groups of rotations, their generator and the invariance of the Laplacian

items.title: The spatial parity action on the component-valued wave-function space
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix an integer $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$, let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ with inner product
linear in the first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$Q_{j},P_{k}$ be the componentwise position and momentum operators
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a)), and
let $\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ and
$W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the componentwise Schwartz and
Sobolev classes ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]],
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Define the **parity action**
$$\bigl(\Pi f\bigr)_{l}(x):=f_{l}(-x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^{3},\ l=1,\dots,r),$$
let $U^{(r)}$ be the unitary momentum representation of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]], and let $M_{-1}$ be
multiplication on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$ by the function
$p\mapsto$ the reflection $g\mapsto g(-p)$, that is $(M_{-1}g)(p):=g(-p)$. Then:

(a) $\Pi$ is a well-defined unitary operator with $\Pi^{2}=\mathrm{id}$ and
$\Pi^{*}=\Pi$; moreover $\Pi\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and
$\Pi W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})=W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$
for $m=1,2$;

(b) $\Pi D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j})$ and $\Pi Q_{j}\Pi=-Q_{j}$; $\Pi D(P_{k})=D(P_{k})$
and $\Pi P_{k}\Pi=-P_{k}$;

(c) $U^{(r)}\Pi U^{(r)-1}=M_{-1}$;

(d) with $H_{0}=\frac{1}{2m_{0}}\sum_{k}P_{k}^{2}$ for a parameter
$m_{0}>0$ and a real bounded measurable $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$, writing
$V_{P}(x):=V(-x)$ and $H_{V}=H_{0}+M_{V}$, one has $\Pi H_{0}\Pi=H_{0}$ and
$\Pi M_{V}\Pi=M_{V_{P}}$, so $\Pi H_{V}\Pi=H_{V_{P}}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice; $r\ge1$;
$\hbar>0$; the space $H^{(r)}$; the componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$;
$f\in H^{(r)}$; $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$; the momentum unitary $U^{(r)}$ and
the multiplier $M_{-1}$; a real bounded measurable $V$; a parameter $m_{0}>0$.

[F1] **Componentwise kinematics.** $Q_{j},P_{k}$ are self-adjoint with the
maximal componentwise domains, $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ lies in both domains and is
invariant under both operators, and on $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ one has $Q_{j}f=x_{j}f$
and $P_{k}f=-i\hbar D_{k}f$ ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]
clauses (a),(c), [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F2] **Momentum representation.** $U^{(r)}$ is unitary with
$U^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(M_{p_{k}})$, $U^{(r)}P_{k}=M_{p_{k}}U^{(r)}$, acting on
Schwartz classes by the componentwise Fourier transform with normalization
$(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}$, and $U^{(r)}\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] clauses (a),(b),
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (b)).

[F3] **Reflection substitution.** For $f\in L^{1}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ one
has $\int f(-x)\,dx=\int f(y)\,dy$, since $x\mapsto-x$ is a linear substitution
of determinant $-1$ and absolute determinant $1$
([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]). A class in $H^{(r)}$
is determined by its components, $\|f\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|^{2}$, and componentwise
operations commute with the $L^{2}$ class formation
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a),
[[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]).

[F4] **Schwartz invariance.** If $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$, then
$\psi_{l}(-\cdot)$ is smooth and $\sup_{x}|x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\psi_{l}(-x)|=\sup_{y}|(-y)^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\psi_{l}(y)|$,
which is finite; hence $\Pi\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and by symmetry
$\Pi\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$ ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F5] **Sobolev and Fourier characterization.** Under the momentum variable
$p=2\pi\hbar\xi$ of [F2], $W^{1,2}$ and $W^{2,2}$ are the sets of classes with
$p_{k}U^{(r)}f\in L^{2}$ for all $k$, respectively with $|p|^{2}U^{(r)}f\in L^{2}$
([[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]],
[[thm-plancherel]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F6] **Density and extension.** $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ is dense in $H^{(r)}$
([[lem-schwartz-space-is-dense-in-l-two]]); a bounded linear operator on a dense
subspace extends uniquely to the whole space ([[thm-extension-of-a-bounded-map-from-a-dense-subspace]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; verify unitarity and involution by the reflection
substitution, transport the action to the momentum representation for the
operator conjugations, and read the Hamiltonian identities off the operator
conjugations.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F6].

1.1 [Unitarity and involution] For $f\in H^{(r)}$ the function $x\mapsto f(-x)$ is measurable with $\int|f_{l}(-x)|^{2}dx=\int|f_{l}(y)|^{2}dy$ by [F3], so the assignment is well defined on classes, linear and isometric; applying it twice returns the original representative, so $\Pi^{2}=\mathrm{id}$, $\Pi$ is bijective and hence unitary with $\Pi^{-1}=\Pi$. Being unitary and an involution, $\Pi$ is also self-adjoint: $\langle\Pi f,g\rangle=\langle f,\Pi g\rangle$ follows by the same substitution, $\Pi^{*}=\Pi$. [F3, given, algebra]

1.2 [Schwartz invariance] [F4] gives $\Pi\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$ directly, with the substitution $y=-x$ used only to identify the reflected exponents. [F4, given]

2.1 [Conjugation of position] Let $f\in H^{(r)}$ and compute $(\Pi Q_{j}\Pi f)_{l}(x)=\bigl(Q_{j}\Pi f\bigr)_{l}(-x)=(-x)_{j}(\Pi f)_{l}(-x)=-x_{j}f_{l}(x)$, so $\Pi Q_{j}\Pi=-Q_{j}$ as an identity of operators with domain $D(Q_{j})$, since $\Pi$ maps $D(Q_{j})$ onto itself (multiplication by $-x_{j}$ is bounded exactly where $x_{j}$ is) and $\Pi^{-1}=\Pi$ by step 1.1. [step 1.1, F1, given, algebra]

2.2 [Momentum-space form] Let $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and compute componentwise with the substitution $y=-x$ of [F3]: $(U^{(r)}\Pi\psi)_{l}(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi_{l}(-x)\,dx=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int e^{ip\cdot y/\hbar}\psi_{l}(y)\,dy=(U^{(r)}\psi)_{l}(-p)=(M_{-1}U^{(r)}\psi)_{l}(p)$. Both $U^{(r)}\Pi U^{(r)-1}$ and $M_{-1}$ are bounded, and they agree on the dense subspace $U^{(r)}\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S^{(r)}$ by [F2]; [F6] extends the identity to all of $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$. [step 1.2, F2, F3, F6, given, algebra]

3.1 [Conjugation of momentum] By [F2] and step 2.2 the conjugate of $P_{k}$ corresponds to $M_{-1}M_{p_{k}}M_{-1}=M_{p_{k}\circ(-\,\mathrm{id})}=M_{-p_{k}}$, because $(M_{-1}M_{p_{k}}M_{-1}g)(p)=p_{k}g(p)\cdot(-1)$; hence $U^{(r)}\,\Pi P_{k}\Pi\,U^{(r)-1}=U^{(r)}(-P_{k})U^{(r)-1}$ and, conjugating by the unitary $U^{(r)}$, $\Pi P_{k}\Pi=-P_{k}$ including domains by [F5] and step 2.2. [step 2.2, F2, F5, given, algebra]

3.2 [Sobolev invariance] By [F5] the sets $W^{1,2},W^{2,2}$ are described by the conditions $p_{k}g\in L^{2}$ and $|p|^{2}g\in L^{2}$ on the momentum representative; by step 2.2 this representative is transformed by $g\mapsto g(-\cdot)$, and $|(-p)|=|p|$ with the coordinate conditions again unchanged; hence $\Pi W^{m,2}=W^{m,2}$ for $m=1,2$. [step 2.2, F5, given, algebra]

4.1 [Hamiltonian conjugation] Since $\Pi P_{k}\Pi=-P_{k}$ with domain preservation by step 3.1 and $\Pi W^{2,2}=W^{2,2}$ by step 3.2, applying the identity twice gives $\Pi P_{k}^{2}\Pi=P_{k}^{2}$ on $W^{2,2}$, hence $\Pi H_{0}\Pi=H_{0}$; and for $f\in H^{(r)}$ one has $(\Pi M_{V}\Pi f)_{l}(x)=V(-x)f_{l}(x)$ by step 1.1, so $\Pi M_{V}\Pi=M_{V_{P}}$ on all of $H^{(r)}$. Adding on the common domain gives $\Pi H_{V}\Pi=H_{V_{P}}$. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F1, given, algebra]

5.1 [Assembly] Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove (a) with step 3.2 for the Sobolev part, steps 2.1, 2.2, 3.1 prove (b) and (c), and step 4.1 proves (d). [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Discrete transformation.** The parity action is an involution, so it has no one-parameter group and no Stone generator; its commutation with the dynamics is decided directly by the conjugation identity $\Pi H_{V}\Pi=H_{V_{P}}$.
- **Scope.** Parity acts on the spatial argument only; no internal-factor sign and no SU(2) lift is introduced.

items.title: Coordinate-rotation generators on the Schwartz classes and their commutators
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix an integer $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$, let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ with the
componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ and the Schwartz class
$\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]],
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]), and let $U(R)$ for $R\in SO(3)$ be
the spatial rotation action of [[lem-nrqm-symmetries-spatial-rotation-action]]
(so that $(U(R)f)(x)=f(R^{-1}x)$ componentwise and $U$ is a strongly continuous
unitary representation). For $i=1,2,3$ define the rotation matrices
$$R_{1}(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos t&-\sin t\\0&\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_{2}(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&0&\sin t\\0&1&0\\-\sin t&0&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_{3}(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t&0\\\sin t&\cos t&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$
put $U_{i}(t):=U(R_{i}(t))$, and let $L_{i}$ be the self-adjoint operator with
$U_{i}(t)=e^{-itL_{i}/\hbar}$ furnished by Stone's theorem
([[thm-stone-one-parameter-unitary-groups]],
[[def-infinitesimal-generator-of-a-unitary-group]]). Then:

(a) for each $i$ the family $t\mapsto U_{i}(t)$ is a strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group with $U_{i}(s+t)=U_{i}(s)U_{i}(t)$ and
$U_{i}(0)=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]);

(b) for every $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ the curve $t\mapsto U_{i}(t)\psi$ is
differentiable at $t=0$ into $H^{(r)}$ with
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}U_{i}(t)\psi=-\sum_{j=1}^{3}(e_{i}\times x)_{j}\,D_{j}\psi,$$
and consequently $\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq D(L_{i})$ and
$$L_{i}\psi=-i\hbar\sum_{j=1}^{3}(e_{i}\times x)_{j}D_{j}\psi=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}\,Q_{j}P_{k}\psi\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)});$$

(c) $L_{i}\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq\mathcal S^{(r)}$ for each $i$, and on
$\mathcal S^{(r)}$ the commutation relations hold:
$$L_{i}L_{k}\psi-L_{k}L_{i}\psi=i\hbar\sum_{j=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ikj}\,L_{j}\psi\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}).$$
No graph-norm density claim (core property in the strict sense) is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice; $r\ge1$;
$\hbar>0$; the space $H^{(r)}$; the componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$; the
rotation action $U$ and the groups $U_{i}$; the generators $L_{i}$; a class
$\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$; real $s,t$ and $h\ne0$.

[F1] **Rotation action.** $(U(R)f)(x)=f(R^{-1}x)$ componentwise defines a
strongly continuous unitary representation of $SO(3)$ on $H^{(r)}$; for $R$ near the identity and $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ the reflected class
$\psi\circ R^{-1}$ is Schwartz, and $R\mapsto U(R)\psi$ is continuous
([[lem-nrqm-symmetries-spatial-rotation-action]] clauses (a),(b),
[[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F2] **Matrices.** $t\mapsto R_{i}(t)$ is a continuous group homomorphism
$(\mathbb R,+)\to SO(3)$ with $R_{i}(0)=I$, $R_{i}(s)R_{i}(t)=R_{i}(s+t)$ and
$R_{i}(t)^{-1}=R_{i}(-t)$; and $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}R_{i}(t)=G_{i}$, where
$G_{1}x=(0,-x_{3},x_{2})$, $G_{2}x=(x_{3},0,-x_{1})$ and $G_{3}x=(-x_{2},x_{1},0)$
for $x\in\mathbb R^{3}$, so that $G_{i}x=e_{i}\times x$. These follow by
direct computation from the addition formulas and the derivatives
$\sin'=\cos$, $\cos'=-\sin$ and the multiplication rules for $3\times3$
matrices ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]],
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]],
[[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]).

[F3] **Componentwise operators and derivatives.** $Q_{j},P_{k}$ are
self-adjoint with maximal componentwise domains, they map $\mathcal S^{(r)}$
into itself, and $D_{j}$ denotes the weak derivative, which on Schwartz classes
agrees with the classical partial derivative
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a),
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F4] **Stone's theorem.** $T\mapsto e^{itT}$ is a bijection from self-adjoint
operators onto strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups, and the domain
$D(T)$ is exactly the set of vectors where $t\mapsto e^{itT}x$ is
differentiable at $0$, with derivative $iTx$
([[thm-stone-one-parameter-unitary-groups]],
[[def-infinitesimal-generator-of-a-unitary-group]]).

[F5] **Schwartz decay and dominated convergence.** For $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ each component and each of its first partial derivatives is bounded and decays faster than any polynomial; hence for fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\psi_{l}(R_{i}(t)^{-1}x)$ is differentiable with derivative $-\sum_{j}(G_{i}x)_{j}(D_{j}\psi_{l})(x)$ at $t=0$, and the difference quotients are dominated by a fixed Schwartz-decaying function near $t=0$ ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]],
[[thm-mean-value-inequality]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]],
[[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F6] **Canonical commutation relations.** On $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ one has
$(Q_{j}P_{k}-P_{k}Q_{j})\psi=i\hbar\delta_{jk}\psi$
([[lem-nrqm-framework-ccr-on-the-schwartz-core]] clause (a)).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; read the group law and continuity from the rotation
representation, differentiate the orbit in the position representation along
the coordinate subgroups, identify the generator with the angular-momentum
expression on Schwartz classes, and compute the commutators from the canonical
commutation relations.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F6].

1.1 [Group law and strong continuity] By [F1], $U_{i}(s+t)=U(R_{i}(s+t))=U(R_{i}(s)R_{i}(t))=U(R_{i}(s))U(R_{i}(t))=U_{i}(s)U_{i}(t)$ using the group law of [F2] and the representation property of [F1]; $U_{i}(0)=U(I)=\mathrm{id}$; each $U_{i}(t)$ is unitary; and strong continuity of $t\mapsto U_{i}(t)\psi$ is the composition of the continuous map $t\mapsto R_{i}(t)$ of [F2] with the continuous orbit map of [F1]. This proves (a). [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 [Differentiation of the orbit on Schwartz classes] Fix $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$, $i$ and one component. By [F2], $R_{i}(h)^{-1}=R_{i}(-h)=I-hG_{i}+O(h^{2})$ entrywise, so $R_{i}(h)^{-1}x=x-hG_{i}x+O(h^{2})$ uniformly for $x$ in a compact set; hence $\psi_{l}(R_{i}(h)^{-1}x)-\psi_{l}(x)=-h\sum_{j}(G_{i}x)_{j}(D_{j}\psi_{l})(x)+o(h)$ pointwise as $h\to0$ by the differentiability of $\psi_{l}$ and the chain rule [F5], with $(G_{i}x)_{j}=(e_{i}\times x)_{j}$ by [F2]. The difference quotients are dominated near $h=0$ by a fixed Schwartz-decaying function because $\psi_{l}$ and its first derivatives decay faster than any polynomial and $|x-hG_{i}x+O(h^{2})|\le2|x|$ for small $h$; dominated convergence [F5] therefore gives convergence in $H^{(r)}$, so the orbit is differentiable at $0$ with the displayed derivative. [F1, F2, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 [Generator on Schwartz classes] By step 1.2 the difference quotient of $t\mapsto U_{i}(t)\psi$ at $0$ converges, so $\psi\in D(L_{i})$ and $-\frac{i}{\hbar}L_{i}\psi=-\sum_{j}(e_{i}\times x)_{j}D_{j}\psi$ by [F4]; multiplying by $i\hbar$ gives $L_{i}\psi=-i\hbar\sum_{j}(e_{i}\times x)_{j}D_{j}\psi$. Since $(e_{i}\times x)_{j}=x_{j'}$ for the two indices $j'$ complementary to $i$ with the signs of [F2], this reads $L_{i}\psi=\sum_{j,k}\varepsilon_{ijk}Q_{j}P_{k}\psi$: for example $L_{3}\psi=-i\hbar(-x_{2}D_{1}+x_{1}D_{2})\psi=x_{1}(-i\hbar D_{2})\psi-x_{2}(-i\hbar D_{1})\psi=(Q_{1}P_{2}-Q_{2}P_{1})\psi$, and the other two cases are the cyclic permutations. This proves (b). [step 1.2, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

3.1 [Invariance of the Schwartz class] The expression $L_{i}\psi=-i\hbar\sum_{j}(e_{i}\times x)_{j}D_{j}\psi$ is a finite sum of products of a linear polynomial with a first weak derivative of a Schwartz class; hence $L_{i}\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ by the closure of $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ under polynomial multiplication and differentiation [F5], so $L_{i}\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq\mathcal S^{(r)}$. [step 2.1, F3, F5, given, algebra]

4.1 [Commutators on the Schwartz class] Let $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ and use the product rule for commutators $[AB,CD]=A[B,C]D+AC[B,D]+[A,C]DB+CA[D,B]$, verified by expanding both sides. By step 2.1, $L_{1}=Q_{2}P_{3}-Q_{3}P_{2}$ and $L_{2}=Q_{3}P_{1}-Q_{1}P_{3}$, and by [F3] all displayed products are defined on $\mathcal S^{(r)}$. Using [F6] and bilinearity, only the terms containing a nonvanishing commutator contribute: $[Q_{2}P_{3},Q_{3}P_{1}]=Q_{2}[P_{3},Q_{3}]P_{1}=-i\hbar Q_{2}P_{1}$, and $[Q_{3}P_{2},Q_{1}P_{3}]=Q_{1}[Q_{3},P_{3}]P_{2}=i\hbar Q_{1}P_{2}$, while $[Q_{2}P_{3},Q_{1}P_{3}]=0$ and $[Q_{3}P_{2},Q_{3}P_{1}]=0$ because in the remaining products every commutator is of coordinate with coordinate or of momentum with momentum, namely $[P_{3},Q_{1}]=[Q_{2},Q_{1}]=[Q_{2},P_{3}]=0$ for the first and $[P_{2},Q_{3}]=[Q_{3},Q_{3}]=[Q_{3},P_{1}]=0$ for the second. Hence $[L_{1},L_{2}]\psi=-i\hbar Q_{2}P_{1}\psi+i\hbar Q_{1}P_{2}\psi=i\hbar(Q_{1}P_{2}-Q_{2}P_{1})\psi=i\hbar L_{3}\psi$. The index triple $(1,2,3)$ and the three coordinate directions enter the definitions of $L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}$ cyclically symmetrically, and the canonical commutation relations are cyclically invariant, so the two cyclic permutations of this computation give $[L_{2},L_{3}]=i\hbar L_{1}$ and $[L_{3},L_{1}]=i\hbar L_{2}$ on $\mathcal S^{(r)}$; that is $[L_{i},L_{k}]\psi=i\hbar\sum_{j}\varepsilon_{ikj}L_{j}\psi$ for all $i,k$. This proves (c). [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, F6, given, algebra]

5.1 [Assembly] Step 1.1 proves (a), steps 1.2 and 2.1 prove (b), and steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove (c); the final clause of the statement records that no graph-norm density statement is made. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Sign and normalization.** All three generators are fixed by the convention $U_{i}(t)=e^{-itL_{i}/\hbar}$ already used for the energy flow; with it, $L_{i}=\sum_{j,k}\varepsilon_{ijk}Q_{j}P_{k}$ on $\mathcal S^{(r)}$, the classical expression $L=x\times p$ read with $P=(-i\hbar D)$.
- **What replaces a core statement.** The lemma proves that the dense subspace $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ lies in every $D(L_{i})$, is mapped into itself by every $L_{i}$ and supports the commutators; the stronger graph-norm density of $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ in $D(L_{i})$ is not asserted here and is not used by the consuming items.
